headline: Airport director outlined a $100 million, five-year improvement plan, a debt restructuring, and a new airline agreement due this fall.
summary: Airport Director Tom Malafronte gave an update on airport finances, capital projects, and air service. Highlights included a $303,000 federal grant for vehicle transponders and a debt restructuring that cut airline operating costs by about $7 million a year. The update was presented for information only.
transcript:
## SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON AIRPORT ACTIVITIES

October 20, 2026 at 4:45 PM

Chairman Burkush called the meeting to order.

The Clerk called the roll.

Present: Aldermen Burkush, Sapienza, Barry, Dexter, Terrio

Messrs.: T. Malafronte

1. Communication from Tom Malafronte, Airport Director, regarding Manchester- Boston Regional Airport's financial, operational, capital improvement, and planning initiatives.

(Note: Provided for informational purposes only; no action is required.)

Tom Malafronte, Airport Director: What I have provided for tonight's update is a memo. I actually updated this a little bit because I had to submit this several weeks ago. So I have a couple of things that I will add to the memo that I initially submitted, and a copy of what is referred to as our airport layout plan, this 11 by 17 drawing. I don't expect you to have to pay attention to all the fine details and all the runway, taxiway and other design criteria. The reason that I provided this is as I'm going through the update and referring to various projects, I just wanted you to have something to refer to. The text boxes are color coded by grant year. So as I go through these projects, the different color codes are for the year the project grant was funded, and generally the same year that the project takes place, there's some anomalies there that I'll talk about. And as I go through this, if you have any questions at all, please stop me. I'm not going to read this memo verbatim, but I'm going to kind of read a couple of the key points here and kind of provide a little background on each one of the bullet points. So the purpose of the memo is to reinforce the fact that we have a coordinated program of financial, operational, capital improvement and planning initiatives that are underway, and the work is intended to reduce airline operating costs, preserve and modernize critical infrastructure, strengthen non-aeronautical revenues, enhance the customer experience and position for future growth. So there's a lot built into that one paragraph, but everything that I'm going to talk about here tonight hits one or all of those points. So first, financial and strategic initiatives. In fiscal year 26, the airport pursued approximately $25 million in federal funding for essential infrastructure and equipment needs. Of the $25 million that we requested, we have already received $10 million and are putting that money to work. There is $15 million remaining through a congressionally directed spending request that we made. That spending request was supported in a letter by Mayor Ruais and also the entire congressional delegation. And basically, what we asked for in that congressionally directed spending request is $15 million for HVAC improvements, the purchase of specialized snow removal equipment, terminal roof replacement and restroom upgrades. And the reason that we did that is because if we can get congressionally directed spending funding to dedicate towards those projects, that $15 million can be funded through a federal grant, as opposed to putting that burden on the back of the airlines and raising their operating costs. So every federal project or every federal grant that we can get to fund projects helps our bottom line, helps the airlines bottom line. That's the reason that we pursued it. The airport also pursued and recently received a grant offer of $303,000. This one is for vehicle transponders. I personally looked into the availability of vehicle transponders many years ago in several positions back as a manager of airport operations and facilities, and at the time the technology hadn't been advanced enough. It was too expensive and there was no federal funding available. So we did not pursue it. As a result, we have equipment that operates on the airfield, that the air traffic control tower and our operations winter snow desk personnel can't see. So at an airport like Manchester that has a category three instrument landing system, we can have airplanes taking off and landing with no visibility. But we also have no visibility over the equipment that we have operating on the runway. So receiving this $303,000 federal grant, again, will not go on the back of the airlines and will allow us enough money to equip 82 vehicles with transponders, so the controllers in the control tower can see all of our vehicles operating during a snowstorm or low visibility this time of year with morning fog, and also the person operating the snow desk. Because, if you can imagine, if you have 30 vehicles operating at one time and you get an airplane on short final, and you need to clear all of those vehicles and 30 vehicles are telling you clear of the runway, are you 100% certain that every single one of those vehicles cleared? So we have several layers and several supervisors that watch that, but to have a visual image and have those transponders in place would be a huge help. So, as soon as we get the grant, we're going to put out an RFP and we're going to get those installed in all of our vehicles. In addition to that, the grant that we pursued through FAA also opened up a separate conversation, and that was about not only seeing vehicles on the airfield, but there was an incident that took place in LaGuardia where Air Canada landed on an active runway and hit a truck that was crossing an active runway to get to the terminal side of the airfield to respond to an incident on another aircraft. So the transponders will be a huge safety enhancement, but to us, it doesn't fix the whole problem. And the problem is when the aircraft rescue firefighting station is located on the opposite side of the airfield as the terminal, then those vehicles have to cross the active runway to respond to 98% of their calls, which are in the terminal building. So that was by design. Nobody made a mistake. Nobody did anything wrong. At airports across the country, the highest value real estate is closer to the terminal. So that's what airports tend to try to lease first. The least valuable is where our aircraft rescue firefighting station, the snow removal equipment, snow storage equipment, things like that. That's where all of that stuff goes. But in light of this accident in LaGuardia and the operations that we see and the records that we have in Manchester, our goal is to get that aircraft rescue firefighting station shifted from the east side of the airfield to the west side of the airfield. So even though the conversation started out around transponders and being able to enhance safety on the airfield, we took advantage of the opportunity to talk with the folks in Washington and say, the real fix for this problem is to relocate the station. The folks in Washington were open to the idea. They forwarded our request/recommendation to the FAA region in Burlington, Mass. We had a conversation at our most recent CIP meeting, and they agreed to actually put it in a future capital improvement program. So it went from a concept to an actual financial plan. We will study it in the master plan. We will cite it in the master plan. Even though I have an idea of where I think it needs to go, it will find its way into the Airport Capital Improvement program. It'll get funded by FAA and eventually it will get built, and it's going to be somewhere in the area of $20 million for a new air facility. But it will greatly enhance safety going forward. For fiscal year 27, the key things that we accomplished are currently underway is first and foremost, the most important thing to me, is the new airline operating agreement. So the airline operating agreement, obviously between us and the airlines and the cargo carriers, expired in June. We're operating under an extension now. We've been kind of going back and forth with the airlines. So the airline operating agreement is complete. So now we're into our final draft, go through all the various legal departments. We'll sign it sometime this fall. And that'll basically get all of our carriers signed on for the next five years. Initially, it's three years with one two year extension, which all of the airlines supported. So that's a critical piece of what we've been doing for the last six months. And we'll finally get that executed this fall, which would be great news for all of us. Debt restructuring, the Board of Mayor and Aldermen approved our request to restructure debt refinance, and some of our bonds. That happened just within the last two weeks. We closed on our debt restructuring. We used $15 million as an estimate. It was a little over $13 million we actually restructured. What that did was reduce the airline's operating costs by about $7 million a year. So if you can imagine if you're Breeze Airways just starting in Manchester, or if you're even Southwest Airlines adding a new flight like Nashville, to reduce their operating costs by $7 million a year was a huge help to them. So obviously we have to spread that debt out over time, but we will go from a $7 million reduction, debt service that was somewhere around $16 million will now be $7 million, and it will drop down to about $4 million in 2036. And by 2043, we'll be completely debt free. So we're going to have to take steps to get there, but it'll help the airlines in the short term. So the airline operating agreement was critical. That's also tied to the debt restructuring. We also are going to initiate a new net metering program. This program is anticipated to reduce energy costs by about $50,000 a year to $75,000 a year, and generate more than $1 million in savings to the airport over the next 20 years. We're in the process of interviewing a couple of energy providers at this point. Vector landing fee collections, if you've never heard of this, there's a company called Vector, and they offer a product called Plane Pass. And what this is is a company that basically tracks landing fees, collects landing fees, so that the airport doesn't have to do it. Right now it's kind of a modified version of the honor system. So the airlines pay, the cargo carriers pay, they self-report, but any corporate general aviation transient aircraft we have no visibility into. So with this company, they will actually track tail numbers, send out invoices. And when this program is up and running, we will bring in about an additional $100,000 a year in landing fees. Every little bit helps.

Alderman Terrio: It's going to bring in an extra $100,000. How much is it going to cost?

T. Malafronte: Vector will get a percentage of the landing fees that they collect. So we won't actually pay out any money. We will give them a percentage of the fees that they bring in. And it's about 8%. So about $8,000 a year to collect $100,000. Terminal advertising and sponsorships, not to get into a lot of detail on that, but we are also opening up additional advertising opportunities, sponsorships. We just recently had developed a deal with Primary Bank. So they are now the sponsor of the business center. Obviously, they were just bought out recently. So that may change in the future. Capital improvements in facilities. So the capital five year capital improvement program identifies and some of them are identified in this 11 by 17, approximately $97 million in airport improvement projects that are funded 90% by FAA, 5% by the state of New Hampshire, 5% by the airport. So for $100 million of improvements over the next five years that we're going to get at the airport, the City of Manchester Department of Aviation is going to pay $5 million of that. So that's a pretty good investment. So everything that you see called out in these text boxes on this airport layout plan, these projects are all part of the $97 million that's been identified for infrastructure improvements that the FAA has agreed to fund, that the state has agreed to fund, and the airport needs to budget for our 5% matching funds. I'll move on to some of those projects that are listed in this handout, which are runway 64 rehabilitation, several taxiway reconstruction projects, terminal facility improvements, and some of the projects that we are either currently working on or recently completed are taxiway Gulf and Delta. Those are the taxiways that are directly behind the terminal building, primarily used by Southwest. That project was completed on September 4th. The design of taxiway echo improvements, I know the diagram is kind of small, but taxiway echo is the taxiway that takes our cargo carriers to and from taxiway echo out to runway 1735 or via taxiway out to runway 624. So when you see on this list taxiway echo improvement, it's a one liner. It doesn't make a lot of headlines. It doesn't seem very exciting, but that one taxiway alone is going to cost somewhere between $13 and $20 million to rehabilitate, because the airplanes that use that taxiway are Airbus 300, 767s, they're all heavy aircraft, and they tend to kind of wear down the taxiway quickly. Airport drainage study is continuing through 2027. Electrical vault expansion will be complete by Q1 of 2027. A new engineered material arresting system, or EMAs, I don't know if any of you recall hearing that term in this room before, but if you remember recently in Miami, an air 21 airplane operating on behalf of Amazon landed long. They did not have any mass pad. They had a standard safety area, but they landed long, left the airfield, went through the perimeter fence, and unfortunately there was a couple of deaths involved. So in Manchester we only have one EMAs pad. At the end of our three runways 1735 and runway six approach ends, we have standard 1000 foot safety areas, so no EMAs pad is required. On the 24 end, and if you've ever driven around that end on Harvey Road, we don't have 1000ft of safety area. In fact, there's a sharp drop off to Harvey Road and then wetland beyond that, thus, the reason that we need to have the EMAs pad. Again, it doesn't seem like a very exciting project, but the replacement of the EMAs pad alone is a $10 million project, federally funded 90% by FAA, 5% by the state. Our pad is now 26 years old, so we're going to replace that in the spring. So you'll be hearing about that project, some other safety improvement enhancements, our new safety management system we're going to implement next spring. I mentioned the vehicle transponders, new snow removal equipment and above all of that, you know, you get this new equipment, new technology, all of that is no good unless you have personnel trained to operate all of it effectively. So we're looking at hosting airport safety and operations specialist training for our airfield personnel, which we did many years ago. I think it's time to offer that again. So there's a couple of other terminal concession renovations that you'll see if you come to the terminal. Queen City Diner, we've renovated and did a ribbon cutting this summer, and Shipyard and Dunkin are also going to be renovated this year. One of the things that just happened recently, I don't think it was in my initial update, but we are also going to be adding new automated exit lanes. So right now when you leave the airport and you go out an exit lane, it's staffed by a contracted security guard. Not the best form of security, not the most reliable form of security, in our opinion. So this is another technology that we've been pursuing for a number of years, we are going to self-fund it. But the return on our investment for putting in this new technology and not paying security guards to staff those exit lanes is three years or less, so definitely worth doing. So you'll start to see that project take place probably end of January, early February. So as you leave the secure area, instead of having a security guard sitting on a chair with a clipboard, you're going to go through those electronic doors like what you see in Nashville and DC, airports like that. Master plan update, the master plan kicked off in May of 2026. A lot of the background work like forecasting inventory, things like that is well underway. We had our first two public meetings on September 23rd and 24th. The meeting on the 23rd was held at Londonderry High School and 24th at Manchester Community College. We'll be having additional meetings as the master plan progresses, and my plan for our next get together is actually to encapsulate where we are in the master plan update, and just kind of give you a quick PowerPoint presentation on all of the inputs that we have so far. Some of the feedback from the community where we think we're heading with the second half of the master plan update, and then the plan is to wrap the entire thing up in 12 to 15 months and have a master plan report that I can hand to all of you in executive summary and a video by Q2 of 2027. So aggressive schedule, a lot to cover, but we're off to a good start. I won't go through all of the committees, but I'll just tell you that the committees, we have three committees that are part of the master plan process. The executive committee is the consulting team and the senior staff at the airport. We kind of guide the process. Study Advisory Committee, which includes Chairman Burkush, Jodie Nazaka from the Economic Development Office, several representatives from the town of Londonderry, from the state, from the business community. So we've got a kind of a good, diverse group of people on that committee. And then the Technical Advisory Committee, the people that tend to stay strictly within their lane, like FAA, TSA, airline representatives, cargo representatives, a public utility, Eversource, concessions, rental car operators, and then the acronym eVTOL, which you've probably seen us or heard us talk about in the past as well. So that is a representative that specifically talks to electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft. So she happens to work for Beta up in Burlington, Vermont. But as part of this master plan, because it looks out as far as 20 years, we need to be prepared for electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating into and out of Manchester. So you need the electrical facilities to be able to support it. You need to have air traffic procedures to be able to get them in and out. So that will be part of the master plan process as well. Then just skipping ahead to commercial development, we continue to pursue public private partnerships and other commercial development. And I'll just give you a couple of examples. You've heard us mention, I think, in the past, Signature Aviation planning to build a new 31,000 square foot hangar with an office facility. That was scheduled for 2027. And as of last week, I learned that they're going to break ground on that facility on November 19th. So that's going to happen this fall. So when Signature grows or the next one, Prostar, is going to build a 41,000 square foot hangar, and that's dependent on contracts with these companies that I list in the memo, more corporate jets, more aircraft maintenance, more avionics, more high paying jobs, more fuel flowage fees to the airport. So anytime we get these developments like this, it's beneficial not only to the corporate and general aviation community, but to the airport as a whole. We're evaluating a number of opportunities with private developers to renovate the Ammon Center. I'll provide, an update on that in our next meeting. The reason that's important to me is the center obviously was built in the early 60s. Right now it's cold storage. It costs the airport $125,000 a year just to keep that building alive. So the plan right now is to hopefully get a developer as part of the master plan process to come along and either want to renovate it or demolish it and build a completely new facility. If we can get a developer that will renovate it, and if we can improve that facility, then what it allows us to do is the fire station that I mentioned in the beginning that we brought to the attention of the FAA in Washington. The region now knows about it. It's going to get built into a capital improvement program and will show up in this 11 by 17. Hopefully, in the next iteration of the CIP. We want to put that building on the north side of the Ammon Center. So we will knock down the north end of the Ammon Center, potentially put a new air facility, renovate the core of the Ammon Center, and build corporate hangars on the other side. When you drive up to the Ammon Center, you're going to see a completely renovated new building. North end will be airport fire station, south end corporate hangars, and the core will be another company. And we're talking with several and hopefully we can make that come to fruition. Land use planning, I won't get into a lot of details on that other than we're talking with the cargo carriers, we're talking with private developers. You get one shot at developing the lands to the highest and best priority. So we're going to try to do that under the master plan, including realigning potentially cargo facilities and opening up some more land for development. But more on that as we go through the master plan. Air service development, I think we've reported on this before, but that traffic in 2025 was up 9% over 2024. We were initially down in passenger traffic because of JetBlue's exit. But because of Southwest adding Nashville and Breeze adding some additional frequencies, we're down 4% year over year, but I think we're going to make that up over the course of the remainder of the fiscal year, based on the loads that we're seeing and the investments that the airlines are making. The most exciting and important information, without going through all of the air service updates, is Southwest announcing new Nashville service, which started on October 1st. So that's their first new destination since 2011, provides a direct connection to a fast growing business and leisure market. To me, what's important about Nashville is not only the little over two hour non-stop flight to get to Nashville, but the fact that you can connect to over 100 cities beyond Nashville. So a year or two from now, if this flight is successful and if the community supports it, we will go back and look at how many people flew directly to Nashville, how many people connected beyond Nashville, and where did they go? And if we see a pattern where enough people are going to Dallas, Denver, Las Vegas, Phoenix, then that's the next nonstop destination that we'll ask for. So it starts with supporting the nonstop that you have. But if we can develop another nonstop because of people connecting through that hub, then it will certainly help. Another big addition that was relatively quiet on the heels of Nashville, was Southwest is going to pick up the Fort Myers service that JetBlue left behind. I think they'll do very well. So they're going to start with the winter months, Saturday only in February, March. So we'll be able to get to go down and watch the Red Sox in spring training. And again, if that is supported seasonally, the season grows. And if it's supported seasonally, then someday you have an opportunity at getting it daily or at least daily seasonal. So again, I won't go through all the details other than to me, the exciting thing is you got American Airlines that still offers up to 15 flights a day. So they're solid. United, several trips a day to Washington. We'd love to have them at another city. Southwest this February is going to be up to 15 flights a day for the first time in about a dozen years. So that's exciting with the addition of Nashville and Fort Myers. Breeze, our last quarterly update for all of our airlines, Breeze led all of the airlines in terms of load factors, so they're filling more seats every day than every other airline at the airport at an average load factor in the last quarter of 92%. They start with two flights a day, 92% could potentially get you to four flights a day, and if the market continues to absorb that, it gets you to daily service. Maybe it's daily, seasonal, depending on the destination. But so far the community has supported Breeze very well. They supported Nashville very well, and we hope that continues because it'll just create more opportunities for us. And then on to customer experience, a couple of things I just wanted to mention, we're expanding options for accessibility and customer service programs. So we've had the explorer program for blind and low vision travelers, American Sign Language for deaf and hard of hearing travelers. We just initiated this summer the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program. And basically, if you're not familiar with that, if anyone in your family has a hidden disability, maybe they're autistic, or maybe they just have anxiety about flying, fear of flying, whatever the case might be, then you can go in and get a lanyard from the communication center or the information booth and get a little extra time, space, patience from the people at the airport who have all been trained in the program. And then a new program I just wanted to give you a little heads up on was Gateside by TSA PreCheck. The program is currently on hold for 30 days. They announced it, pulled it back, but it's going to come back online. And what that is, is if you have someone coming to arrive at the airport and you want to go out to the gate to meet them, or if you want to see maybe a young person or a parent or something like that, out at the gate as they leave, you're going to be able to do that. You go online, you sign up just like you would for PreCheck, and you can get a gate pass that you can actually get access to the gate. It'll help our concessions. It'll help our airlines. It'll help our customers. Along those lines, we were just recently recognized two days ago by the Future Insight Organization as their Q4 recipient of the first Site Access Award. And this is in recognition of the airport's continuing efforts to make air travel more accessible. So that just happened this week. And then looking ahead for the remainder of fiscal year 27, what are we going to be focused on? On the days that you don't see me and the members of the airport team, we're going to continue to work through the airport master plan process. I'm going to provide an update probably halfway through the process once we get more input so you know exactly where we're headed. Coordinate and complete critical airport capital improvement projects, which are all identified on this airport layout plan. And again, this is not to be taken lightly. It's $100 million in airport improvements that we're going to put into this airport over the next five years. Work to align staff with the future needs of the airport. I spoke with Chairman Burkush just briefly, so I want to publicly thank each and every one of you and thank the full board for approving, it seems like a minor thing, asking for an Accountant I to be upgraded to an Accountant II, or asking for a starting pay rate to be a step 7 instead of a step 3 or 4. It seems incremental, but it's tremendously helpful to us in getting the right person with the right qualifications and the right attitude into the right job. Because in an airport like Manchester, you're not going to just work in your lane, you're going to be cross trained, you're going to work in other lanes, and there's no job description that we have that can quite describe that. So allowing us the flexibility to do that, we've brought on some really good people that are excited to be at the airport. And my job, my goal, is to position the airport for the next generation of people that are walking in the door today, and you're helping us do that. So thank you for that. We're also going to start working on our airport 100 year anniversary celebration, which happens to be June 7th of 2027. We'll have one key day where we honor the 100 year anniversary of the airport, and then we'll do a number of things throughout the year to honor the history of the airport, the military history, the civilian history, and both then continue to lay the groundwork and position the airport for the next century of flight. And as I said, the next update will be geared specifically towards what we've finished on all of these projects that I've mentioned here today and where we're going with the airport master plan.

Alderman Terrio: This might be beyond the scope of this meeting, and you can catch me offline, but I see there's an airfield drainage study. We've been talking a lot lately, I know you guys have fuel, firefighting chemicals, and you're right on the Merrimack River. Do you monitor for runoff into the river?

T. Malafronte: We do. We have an environmental company that works directly for us. We do quarterly visual monitoring, and then we monitor every time there's a de-icing event.

Chairman Burkush: Thank you for the presentation.

There being no further business, on motion of Alderman Sapienza , duly seconded by

Alderman Dexter , it was voted to adjourn.

A True Record. Attest.

Clerk of Committee
